summary: This document describes conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the CMS key package receipt and error content types. It covers SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, and AuthEnvelopedData.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains which locks and seals to use on the key delivery receipt notes.

subtitle: Which signature, key-transport and encryption algorithms to support when protecting CMS key package receipts and errors.

tldr.problem: RFC 7191 defines key package receipt and error content types carried in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), but implementers need to know which algorithms to support so that their messages interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7192 lists required and recommended algorithms for each CMS protection type (SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthEnvelopedData) and the minimum public key sizes. It defines no new algorithms.
tldr.outcome: Implementations get a common baseline: RSA with SHA-256 for signatures, AES-128 in CBC mode for content encryption, AES-GCM for authenticated encryption, and keys of 1024 to 2048 bits.

today: RFC 7192 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
RFC 7192 describes the conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) key package receipt and error content types defined in RFC 7191. It covers four CMS protection types: SignedData, EnvelopedData and EncryptedData from RFC 5652, and AuthEnvelopedData from RFC 5083.

The document does not define any new algorithms. It points to algorithms that are already defined elsewhere. Its requirements match those in RFC 5959, RFC 6033, RFC 6160, RFC 6161 and RFC 6162, with two exceptions: the content-encryption algorithm is AES in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode rather than AES Key Wrap with Message Length Indicator (MLI), and the key-wrap algorithm is plain AES Key Wrap rather than the MLI variant.

The reason is that receipts and errors are not keys, so AES Key Wrap with MLI is not appropriate for encrypting them. The RFC also notes that RFC 7191 only requires the key package receipt to be signed.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a rulebook that says which secret codes to use when sending a receipt. It does not invent new codes. It picks from codes that already exist.

sections.title: SignedData
sections.content:
If an implementation supports SignedData, it MUST support the RSA signature scheme. It SHOULD also support the RSA Probabilistic Signature Scheme (RSASSA-PSS) and the Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA).

Implementations MUST support the hash function SHA-256 alongside these signature schemes, and SHOULD support SHA-1. They can also choose to support the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA).

Since RFC 7191 requires receipts to be signed, this is the section that matters most for receipts.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is like signing your name on a letter so people know it is really from you. Everyone must know the most common way of signing, and may know a few others.

sections.title: EnvelopedData
sections.content:
If an implementation supports EnvelopedData, it MUST implement key transport and MAY implement key agreement. With key transport, RSA encryption MUST be supported and RSAES-OAEP SHOULD be supported. With key agreement, ephemeral-static Diffie-Hellman MUST be supported and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) MAY be supported.

Whichever key management technique is used, implementations MUST support AES-128 in CBC mode as the content-encryption algorithm and SHOULD support AES-256 in CBC mode.

When key agreement is used, the key lengths must line up. If the content-encryption algorithm is AES-128 in CBC mode, the key-wrap algorithm MUST be AES-128 Key Wrap. If it is AES-256 in CBC mode, the key-wrap algorithm MUST be AES-256 Key Wrap.
sections.plainLanguage: An envelope hides a message so only the right person can open it. There are two ways to hand over the key to the envelope, and the rules say which ways everyone must know.

sections.title: EncryptedData
sections.content:
If an implementation supports EncryptedData, it MUST implement AES-128 in CBC mode and SHOULD implement AES-256 in CBC mode.

EncryptedData requires that keys be managed by other means. Because of that, the only algorithm this section specifies is the content-encryption algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the lock is chosen, but how you get the key to the other person is somebody else's problem.

sections.title: AuthEnvelopedData
sections.content:
If an implementation supports AuthEnvelopedData, it MUST follow the EnvelopedData recommendations, except for the content-encryption algorithm. For this type the content-encryption algorithm MUST be AES-GCM. The 128-bit version MUST be implemented and the 256-bit version SHOULD be implemented.

Implementations MAY also support AES-CCM.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an envelope that also has a tamper seal, so you can tell if someone changed the message inside. A different lock is used because it has to do both jobs.

sections.title: Public Key Sizes
sections.content:
The easiest way to implement SignedData, EnvelopedData and AuthEnvelopedData is with public key certificates, as defined in RFC 5280.

If an implementation supports RSA, RSASSA-PSS, DSA, RSAES-OAEP or Diffie-Hellman, it MUST support key lengths from 1024 bits to 2048 bits, inclusive. If it supports ECDSA or ECDH, it MUST support keys on the P-256 curve.
sections.plainLanguage: A longer key is like a lock with more tumblers. Everyone has to be able to handle locks in a certain range of sizes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3370, RFC 3394, RFC 3560, RFC 4056, RFC 5084, RFC 5652, RFC 5753 and RFC 5754 apply.

The RFC also points to NIST SP 800-57, which gives comparable bits of security for some algorithms and key sizes, along with time frames during which certain numbers of bits of security are appropriate. Some environments may find those time frames useful.
sections.plainLanguage: The safety rules for each lock are written down in the documents that define the locks. This one just tells you to read them.
